1:
Clarke finds a delicacy in the original not often observed: the Hebrew is Adam born of woman, few of days, and full of tremor. The first Adam did not spring from woman and lived nine hundred and thirty years; the Adam who now springs from woman by ordinary generation has seventy at the outside. He seems born, Clarke concludes, not indeed to live but to die, and by living forfeits the title to life. Gill starts from the same distinction and uses it differently, noting that the first man was made out of the dust and not born of a woman, and that Job chiefly designs himself. Delitzsch grounds the frailty in the birth itself: the woman is weak, brings forth in pain, and is impure in her lying-in, so weakness, suffering and impurity are man's portion from the birth. Henry takes "born of a woman" either of Eve, first in the transgression, or of each man's immediate mother, on the maxim that the child takes after the mother; let not the strong man glory in his strength, since when God pleases the mighty men become as women.

Ellicott alone questions where the verse begins, joining it to the close of the preceding chapter as one continuous sentence, so that the rotten thing that consumeth is the man born of woman who came forth as a flower and was cut off. Job, having just resolved to come into judgment with God, is picturing the miserable creature with whom God will have to contend.

Verse 4 divides them on grammar, not doctrine. Gill, Henry, Clarke and Wesley all take it as a rhetorical question about inherited corruption, and Clarke stacks the versions behind them: the Chaldee asks who will produce a clean thing from man polluted with sins except God who is one, Coverdale answers with "No body", and the Codex Alexandrinus adds that none is pure from corruption though he had lived one day upon the earth. Henry's image for it is legal and medical at once: our blood is not only attainted by a conviction but tainted with an hereditary disease. Ellicott suggests the clause may not be a question at all but a wish: oh that the clean could come forth from the unclean, but none can.

The real disagreement is at verse 5, and it does not fall along the usual lines. Henry states the determinist reading at its strongest: the number of our months is with God, the bounds he has fixed we cannot pass, and we are no more governed by the Stoic's blind fate than by the Epicurean's blind fortune. Wesley agrees that a certain end is appointed beyond which a man cannot prolong life, and Gregory generalises it: nothing happens to men without the secret counsel of Almighty God, who decreed before the ages of the world how all things should be ordered. Clarke, of Wesley's school, denies it. He first empties the alchemists' promise of an elixir, listing Geber, Van Helmont, Paracelsus and Artephius among its claimants, observing that all are dead and some comparatively young, and that the ninety years credited to Artephius became nine hundred only when a disciple added a cipher. Then the consequence: the bounds apply to the race in general and not to individuals, since folly and wickedness plainly abridge a man's term, and the contrary supposition involves innumerable absurdities.

Gregory reads the two measures of verse 5 as pulling opposite ways. The days are short and ours; the months are multiplied and are with God, so the counting of months is itself a sign that the life is further extended afterwards. At verse 6 Ellicott turns the hireling's day the same way, rendering "accomplish" rather as have pleasure in, so Job asks not that the man finish his work but that he rejoice at the day when his wages are paid him.
7:
The tree turns on a point of botany, and Gill and Clarke have checked it and disagree. Gill will not overstate it: the laurel, he says on Pliny's authority, rises into a new body and the willow produces new sprouts, but the cypress when cut down never sprouts any more, unless in one place, in Aenaria. Since it is the case of some, that is sufficient to Job's purpose. Clarke, following Calmet, pushes the other way: some trees grow from cuttings, some revive on being replanted though their roots have withered in the sun, and some have fibres so solid that after several years in water the blossoms expand again, as he says he has often witnessed in the rose of Jericho. Few trees, he concludes, will not send forth new shoots when the stock is cut down level with the earth.

Henry grades the kinds of life instead. Vegetable life is a cheap and easy thing, and the scent of water will recover it; animal life, in some insects and fowls, is retrieved by the heat of the sun; but the rational soul, once retired, is too great and too noble to be recalled by any of the powers of nature, out of the reach of sun or rain and restorable only by the immediate operations of Omnipotence.

Verse 10 sets two Hebrew words for man side by side, and Henry and Wesley read them identically: Geber the mighty man dies though mighty, and Adam the man of earth returns to it, wasting before death, giving up the ghost in death, and afterwards not where he was, his place knowing him no more. Gill turns the same word into a roll-call of those who die anyway, the wise and the rich alike. Delitzsch renders the verb in the neuter: the man lies there stretched out, fallen together and gone without a trace of life. Clarke answers the closing question with the Persian poet Khosroo, who wept at the burying ground, asked where his friends were, and had the question given back by an echo.

Verse 11 is where they part. Ellicott denies there is a comparison at all: the Hebrew has no particle denoting comparison, the water never fails from the sea, great rivers like the Nile never dry up, and the relation implied but not expressed is one of contrariety, so that sooner shall the sea fail and the rivers become dry than the man who has lain down shall arise. He blames the Authorised Version's "as" for obscuring it; Gill, who offers the same rendering without the "as", half agrees. Wesley keeps the simile plainly: when the sea forsakes its place, the river fed by it dries up beyond recovery. Clarke reads it as evaporation and makes it a consolation: the vapours condense, fall as rain and return by the rivers, and though each man is imperceptibly removed the race is kept up by perpetual generations.

How much of the resurrection is in the passage divides them further. Henry holds it was doubtless an article of Job's creed, and reads the lying down as meaning only that no man rises to such a world and such a state as this. Clarke says it would be difficult to twist the passage into a denial of the resurrection of the body, or into a belief that the soul is material and sleeps until it. He quotes the epitaph on Bion, where the mallows and garden herbs wake again but the great and the wise sleep the endless sleep, calls it the most cold and comfortless philosophy ever invented, and points to the next verse as proof that Job did not hold it. Ellicott concedes less: there is no hope of a future life here and still less of a resurrection, though the language is no absolute denial either, and an unexpressed longing seems to glimmer through it.
13:
Gill takes the request literally and lists where Job might be hidden: in the chambers the prophet speaks of, in Hades where the dead are insensible of the calamities on the earth, or in some cavern in the utmost recesses of it. His conclusion is startling: the wish is to be buried alive rather than upon earth with such misery. Clarke splits the verse in two, giving the first clause to the body and the second to the spirit: hide my soul with thyself, where my enemies cannot invade my repose, and my body in the tomb. The set time, he insists, must be the resurrection: what else could be an object of desire to one whose body is mingled with the dust? Wesley keeps the grave as both resting-place and hiding-place, where God hides his own as we hide treasure in a place of secrecy and safety.

Everything then turns on one word in verse 14. Clarke takes "my change" as renovation, the word used of the springing again of grass after it has withered, and calls that in itself a very expressive emblem of the resurrection; he finds in it no doubt at all but a strong persuasion of the general resurrection, and lines the versions up behind it, the Greek giving "I will endure till I live again". Ellicott renders the same word as the transition from life to death, so Job hopes all the days of his warfare, until he dies, that God will call and he will answer. Wesley is with Ellicott, waiting patiently for the change that will put a period to his calamities. Yet Ellicott concedes the other reading in a question: why ask whether a man shall live again if it were absolutely certain that he would not? Gill adds that the Targum narrows the question to the wicked.

At verse 15 Gill will not choose between death and the resurrection and expounds both: the summons that reaches a dying man by some distemper rather than by a prophet, and the call that raised Lazarus. Clarke has no such hesitation, hearing the voice that says there shall be time no longer, awake, ye dead. His point is the verb for desire, which he renders thou wilt pant with desire, or yearn over the work of thy hands: even God is earnestly longing for the reviviscence of the sleeping dust.

The bag of verse 17 Gill alone reads two opposite ways. Either the transgression is sealed up away from Job, so that he is entirely ignorant of what he is afflicted for, or God has bagged and sealed his sins so that none is lost and all may be produced against him another day. Clarke prefers the second and reaches for the news, noting that as he writes in July 1820 charges of state transgressions sealed up in a green bag and laid before both houses of parliament are making a considerable noise in the land; he adds that others take it of money sealed up in bags. Delitzsch rejects the suggestion that what is sealed is the judge's sentence, waiting only to be handed over for execution.

Henry and Wesley end by rebuking the speaker. Henry allows that Job does right to the divine justice in owning that he smarted for his sins, but wrong to the divine goodness in suggesting that God was extreme to mark what he did amiss; it was unadvisedly said, and Henry declines to dwell upon it, adding that God seals up the transgression of the impenitent but blots out his people's sins as a cloud. Wesley puts it in four words: herein Job speaks rashly. Clarke removes the occasion for the rebuke by construing the opening particle as concessive: although thou numberest my steps, and though thou seemest bent on my utter destruction, yet thou delightest in mercy and I shall be saved.
18:
Henry and Clarke reach for the same Latin tag at verse 19: the waters wear the stones not by violence but by falling often; Clarke adds a second form of it: from frequent dropping, perpetually falling, even a stone is hollowed into a hole. Henry draws from it that on this earth everything is the worse for the wearing, time devouring all things, and adds that it is not so with the heavenly bodies. Wesley runs the series together as one figure: the mountain moulders away like a fading leaf, the rock thrown down is never re-advanced, the worn stones can never be made whole, the herbs and fruits washed away by a flood are irrecoverably lost, and in like manner, when a man dies, all hope of his living again in this world is gone. Gill notices that the mountain does not merely fall but dissolves over the ground it destroys, never gathered up into a mountain again. Ellicott holds the passage together differently, reading verses 16 to 22 as one continuous complaint: persecution so persistent would wear out the strongest, even as the mountain and the rock are gradually worn away, and how much more must the speaker be subject to decay.

At verse 20 Delitzsch takes issue with the older expositors. They explained the verb as "thou provest thyself stronger than he" because the root is intransitive, but Delitzsch shows it is transitive too, in the sense of seizing forcibly and grasping, and renders it "Thou seizest him for ever". The many sufferings God inflicts in the course of a life, he adds, are not what the verse means. Gill takes the simpler line: God is more than a match for man in everything, disease is his messenger and goes at his command, and death reigns with a despotic power over all men in all ages.

On the changed countenance Henry and Clarke part. Henry sees two changes, from the disease of the body and from the discomposure of the mind, since the approach of death will make the strongest and stoutest change countenance. Clarke suspects an allusion to the custom of covering a condemned man's face before sending him to execution, as with Haman.

Verse 21 they read alike but apply differently. Clarke says the dead man is equally indifferent whether his children met with a splendid or an oppressive lot, since in that day all his thoughts perish; Wesley allows either that he is ignorant of such events or that he is not affected with them. Henry turns it into counsel: the dying man is a perfect stranger to the things that once filled him, and this should moderate our cares for our families, since God will know what comes of them when we are gone.

The last verse is the hardest, and Clarke lays out the options rather than settling them. The Chaldee has the flesh grieving over the man on account of the worms and the soul wailing in the house of judgment, or, in another copy, grieving before the window is closed over him; another rendering has the flesh dropping away from him and the soul becoming a waste. The version Clarke calls the most natural makes flesh and breath conscious beings, the flesh lamenting its putrefaction in the grave and the breath mourning over the mouldering clay it once enlivened. Coverdale keeps it to this life: while a man liveth his flesh must have travail. Gill hesitates between the pains of the sick and dying bed, which would explain the indifference of the verse before, and Aben Ezra's reading, which takes the flesh upon him of the body rotting in the grave. Henry keeps the dying man in view and draws the moral: dying work is hard work and dying pangs commonly sore pangs, so it is folly to defer repentance to a death-bed.
